docs.title: Why does MemTile need 4D addressing?
docs.text:
The XDNA MemTile DMA path does not preserve a plain row-major matrix after a tile is packed. Step 2 writes each incoming mct × kmt slab as consecutive mct × kct blocks. Step 3 must therefore identify both the packed kct tile and the strip inside that tile.

For a strip width s, the required traversal has four independent indices:

(b, u, i, v)

where b selects the packed kct tile, u selects the s-wide strip within that tile, i selects a row, and v selects an element within the strip.

The physical address is:

addr = b · (mct · kct) + u · s + i · kct + v

Here b cannot be folded into the outer strip counter: crossing a kct tile changes the physical base by the full packed tile size.

docs.title: Interactive demonstration
docs.text:
The self-contained animation below walks through the three stages:

  1. ShimTile MM2S reads a row-major mct × K tile.
  2. MemTile S2MM packs it into consecutive mct × kct blocks.
  3. MemTile MM2S compares the required 4D traversal with an incorrect 3D model.

docs.title: Why 3D fails
docs.text:
A 3D descriptor can describe the first strip and may appear correct while the stream remains inside one packed tile. It fails at the first kct-tile boundary because it has no independent counter for the packed tile base. An exhaustive search over possible 3D affine shapes cannot reproduce the required address sequence for the non-degenerate proof configuration.

The demo’s 3D vs 4D control shows the first mismatch, while Exhaustive 3D search checks every possible factorization for the current parameters.

docs.title: amdgpu
docs.text: Notes from the allbilly/amdgpu repository, which explores direct PM4 compute submission and trap-handler debugging on AMD GPUs.

docs.title: What is implemented
docs.text:
The proof-of-concept opens a DRM render node, initializes libdrm_amdgpu, allocates GPU buffer objects, maps them into the GPU virtual address space, uploads a raw shader, emits PM4 compute packets, submits an indirect buffer and waits for a fence.

The repository also includes register access through debugfs regs2, an offscreen RADV triangle reference, raw GFX PM4 experiments and small GCN shader examples.

docs.title: Build and run
docs.text:
On a Fedora-like system:

sudo dnf install libdrm-devel clang llvm vulkan-tools \
  mesa-vulkan-drivers vulkan-headers vulkan-loader-devel
make
build/amdgpu-poc --card /dev/dri/renderD128

Compile the shader examples for the tested Renoir target:

AMDGPU_MCPU=gfx90c make shaders
build/amdgpu-poc --shader build/add-output.bin --pass-output-va \
  --output-bytes 16

The expected first output bytes are 05 00 00 00, representing 2 + 3 = 5 in little-endian form. A multiply example writes 42 from 6 × 7.

docs.title: Driver reference path
docs.text: The project uses RADV through the normal Vulkan loader as a known-good triangle reference before comparing the resulting command stream with direct GFX PM4 submission. The tested local GPU is AMD Renoir with LLVM target gfx90c.

docs.title: nvgpu
docs.text: Notes from the allbilly/nvgpu repository, which runs a small CUDA-style add kernel on an RTX 3080 eGPU using a handwritten Python userspace stack.

docs.title: What is implemented
docs.text:
The live path reimplements the userspace pieces needed to boot the GPU System Processor (GSP), create channels, build a GPFIFO launch, upload a hand-built SM86 cubin, and execute the kernel. It does not import the tinygrad runtime on the live path; tinygrad is retained only as a reference for constants and health checks.

The cubin contains a small vector operation with four floating-point additions, two loads and one store. On Linux, the hardware boundary is the open NVIDIA kernel interface; on macOS, the project uses the TinyGPU helper for PCIe and BAR access.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
The offline self-test checks cubin construction and launch-word generation without requiring an eGPU:

python3 examples/middle_nv.py --middle-selftest

With the RTX 3080 eGPU attached:

python3 examples/add.py

The expected result is:

[11.0, 22.0, 33.0, 44.0]

The repository reports that device setup and GSP boot dominate the runtime; the small add kernel itself takes only a few milliseconds.

docs.title: CUDA tools on macOS
docs.text:
macOS cannot run NVIDIA CUDA tools natively. The project uses Docker for tools such as nvdisasm, without GPU passthrough:

python3 -c "import examples.middle_nv as a; open('add.cubin','wb').write(a.build_cubin())"
docker run --rm --platform linux/amd64 -v "$PWD":/work -w /work \
  nvidia/cuda:12.4.1-devel-ubuntu22.04 nvdisasm add.cubin

docs.title: RK3588 Mali GPU
docs.text: Notes from the allbilly/rk3588gpu repository, which brings up the RK3588 Mali GPU from Python by opening the device, issuing ioctls and submitting work without libmali or Mesa in the direct path.

docs.title: Two driver paths
docs.text:
The repository documents both GPU stacks found on RK3588 systems:

Stack Device Submission path Panthor mainline /dev/dri/renderD128 DRM Panthor ioctls and a CSF stream Proprietary kbase /dev/mali0 Mali kbase CSF ioctls

On many vendor images, /dev/mali0 is the Mali GPU while renderD128 belongs to the display subsystem. The correct device node therefore depends on the kernel and driver stack installed on the board.

docs.title: Submission flow
docs.text:
The kbase path follows this sequence:

Python → VERSION_CHECK / SET_FLAGS → global interface query
       → queue group creation → memory allocation → command-stream fill
       → queue kick → Mali G610 → completion event

Captured .mcap traces can be decoded and replayed, while the command-stream disassembler exposes the CSF words used by the examples.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
For the mainline Panthor path:

python3 examples/add.py
python3 examples/add.py --dry-run -v

The standalone vector-add example is expected to produce [11, 22, 33, 44]. For a vendor kbase device, the repository provides capture and replay tools:

python3 experiemental/tools/mcap.py gen-sample -o /tmp/test.mcap
python3 experiemental/replay.py /tmp/test.mcap --dry-run

Live replay requires /dev/mali0 and suitable video or render group permissions. A GPU reset or reboot may be required after a fatal command-stream error.

docs.title: Apple ANE
docs.text: Notes from the allbilly/ane repository, which runs Apple Neural Engine operations from pure Python on M1 Asahi Linux. The project programs the NPU directly and does not depend on Espresso, Core ML, Metal, .mlmodel files, or private Apple APIs.

docs.title: Status and platform
docs.text: The project is tested on Apple Silicon running Asahi Linux. The documented bring-up path requires an ANE-enabled Asahi kernel and kernel module (KMD), so these examples are intended for an Apple Silicon Linux installation rather than a normal macOS environment.

docs.title: Supported operations
docs.text:
The example programs cover:

ADD  MUL  MIN  MAX  SUMSQ  CONV  CONCAT  GEMM  RELU  SIGMOID

With the kernel support installed, basic examples can be run with Python:

pip install numpy
python examples/elementwise.py add
python examples/elementwise.py mul
python examples/conv.py
python examples/concat.py
python examples/gemm.py
python examples/relu.py
python examples/sigmoid.py

NumPy is used by many examples but is optional in the core approach.

docs.title: Execution paths
docs.text:
There are two complementary ways to run an operation:

  1. Compile a model with anecc into an .ane file, then run it through the Python binding.
  2. Extract the command buffer from an HWX file and replay it directly from Python, without an .ane file or anecc.

The repository’s experimental/hwx2.py tool generates a readable Python program from an HWX file:

python experimental/hwx2.py hwx/sum.hwx -o sum_from_hwx.py
python sum_from_hwx.py

This makes the register programming and command-buffer layout inspectable.

docs.title: Example: convolution
docs.text:
The repository demonstrates convolution both through a compiled .ane model and through direct register programming. The direct examples use the same firmware and kernel data, and are intended to produce identical results.

The input layout is significant: the examples use a stride of 32 between channels, matching the firmware’s expected layout. Kernel data must also be byte-exact; an incorrectly positioned weight blob can make output channels appear to be zero even when the register setup is otherwise correct.

docs.title: Kernel setup
docs.text:
The repository documents building an Asahi kernel with ANE support and installing the KMD. The high-level flow is:

git clone https://github.com/AsahiLinux/linux.git --branch fairydust --single-branch
make -j$(nproc)
make dtbs -j$(nproc)
sudo make modules_install
sudo make dtbs_install
sudo make install
sudo reboot

After booting the new kernel, the ANE module and device should be available before running the examples. See the repository README for the exact kernel patches, device-tree details and recovery steps for kernel updates.

docs.title: NVDLA
docs.text: Notes from the allbilly/nvdla repository, which explores pure register programming on the NVDLA neural processing unit.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
The repository uses the NVDLA virtual platform to test loadable programs and compare direct register programming with the reference runtime:

docker run -it --rm -p 6667:6667 \
  -v ./examples/vp:/usr/local/nvdla/vp:z \
  -v ./examples:/usr/local/nvdla/examples:z \
  -w /usr/local/nvdla/ \
  onnc/vp aarch64_toplevel -c aarch64_nvdla.lua

ssh -p 6667 root@127.0.0.1
mount -t 9p -o trans=virtio r /mnt
cd /mnt && insmod drm.ko && insmod opendla.ko
./nvdla_runtime --loadable test_Add.nvdla --image input1x5x7.pgm --rawdump

The Python examples include simple add, convolution and 1×1 convolution experiments:

python3 examples/simple_add.py
python3 examples/conv.py
python3 examples/conv_1x1x8.py

docs.title: Loadable parsing
docs.text:
An NVDLA loadable can be inspected with:

python3 parse.py examples/vp/test_Add.nvdla

The repository uses this to connect the serialized loadable format with the register programming needed by the virtual platform.

docs.title: Capture caveat
docs.text: The logging kernel module is useful for capturing registers, but its submit path is not the validation path. First confirm that the operation works with opendla.ko; then use the logging module for investigation. The README also notes that verbose buffer dumping can be slow and may leak temporary GEM handles during long capture runs.

docs.title: RK3588 NPU
docs.text: This page collects notes from the allbilly/rk3588 README, a pure-Python project for running operations on the RK3588 NPU through register programming. It does not use RKNN or a compiler.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
The NPU is organized as a pipeline. CNA handles convolution input and weights, CORE performs MAC-array accumulation, DPU handles output and elementwise processing, and PPU handles pooling. PC controls operation enable, while RDMA feeds elementwise data in parallel.

┌─────────┐    ┌─────────┐    ┌─────────┐    ┌─────────┐    ┌─────────┐
│   CNA   │───▶│  CORE   │───▶│   DPU   │───▶│   PPU   │───▶│   PC    │
│ Conv    │    │ Compute │    │ Output  │    │ Pooling │    │ Control │
└─────────┘    └─────────┘    └─────────┘    └─────────┘    └─────────┘
                    ▲
                    │
                 RDMA

The programming model is hierarchical: multiple submits contain multiple tasks, and each task can contain multiple operations. A task can fuse work such as convolution, elementwise operations, batch normalization, bias shift, ReLU and pooling.

docs.title: Task configuration
docs.text:
The main enable-mask values are:

Block Mask PPU RDMA 0x40 PPU 0x20 DPU 0x10 CORE 0x08 CNA 0x04 PC 0x01

Typical combinations from the project are:

CONV             0x0d = CORE | CNA | PC
GEMM/elementwise 0x18 = DPU  | CORE
POOL             0x60 = PPU_RDMA | PPU

The task interrupt mask is commonly 0xc00 or 0x300, and the operation index used by the examples is 1 for convolution and 4 for GEMM.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
The examples are self-contained Python programs. On an Orange Pi Ubuntu image with the vendor RKNPU driver installed:

pip install numpy
python examples/elementwise.py
python examples/gemm.py
python examples/conv.py
python examples/conv_gemm.py

On mainline Armbian with the ROCKET driver:

python examples/kernel6_18/conv.py
python experimental/kernel6_18/elementwise.py
python experimental/kernel6_18/gemm.py
python experimental/kernel6_18/pool.py

The project reports testing on an Orange Pi 5 16 GB, Orange Pi Ubuntu 1.2.2 with Linux 6.1.99, and Armbian Ubuntu 24.04 with a 6.18 Rockchip kernel.

docs.title: PC chaining and multicore
docs.text:
PC chaining allows multiple operations to run within one submit, reducing submit overhead. The project demonstrates this in the GEMM, convolution and pool examples. Large matrix multiplications can be split along the N dimension and chained into one submit.

The RK3588 has three NPU cores. Different operations—or partitions of a GEMM— can run on separate cores. Multicore support is still marked work in progress in the source project; its current example is:

python experimental/pool_multicore.py

docs.title: Matmul through convolution
docs.text:
The RK3588 NPU is NVDLA-based and designed around convolution. The project maps matrix multiplication onto a 3D 1×1 convolution:

C(M,N) = A(M,K) × B(K,N)

Input feature map A:  H=M, W=1, C=K
Convolution kernel B: N kernels, R=1, S=1, C=K
Output feature map C: H=M, W=1, C=N

Each input row A[m, :] becomes a feature-map position, each output column B[:, n] becomes a convolution kernel, and the resulting output satisfies:

C[m, n] = Σ A[m, k] · B[k, n]

docs.title: Register notes
docs.text:
The project identifies these common target blocks:

Target Block 0x0201 CNA / convolution front-end 0x0801 CORE / MAC array 0x1001 DPU / output and elementwise 0x2001 RDMA 0x0081 PC / operation enable

For detailed register fields, examples and driver comparisons, see the upstream README and the project’s experimental/rockchip.py implementation.
